sections.heading: Key facts
sections.text:
• Standardized global estimation of gambling harms has been limited, but estimates suggest that 1.2% of the world’s adult population has a gambling disorder. Harm from gambling by others is also widespread.

• Industry analysts estimate global gambling revenue will reach US$ 700 billion by 2028 (1) . Smartphone use in low- and middle-income countries will drive much of this growth.

• People gambling at harmful levels generate around 60% of losses (gambling revenue) (2) .

• Gambling can threaten health, leading to increased incidence of mental illness and suicide. It can drive poverty by diverting household spending from essential goods and services.

• Gambling harms also include relationship breakdown, family violence, financial distress, stigma, income-generating crimes (theft, fraud), neglect of children, and erosion of civil institutions via corruption and corporate political activity. Gambling is also a common way to launder money obtained through illegal activities.

• The rapid normalization of gambling is occurring through commercialization and digitization. Sponsorship and marketing are also key factors in rapid global growth.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
Gambling is risking money (or another item of value) on an event of uncertain outcome, with the possibility of gaining an increased return. Betting, slot machines, casino games, lotteries and bingo are all forms of gambling. Electronic gambling machines (EGMs) and casino games are often associated with the most risk of harm. These are available both in physical venues and online. The legal status of gambling varies within and between countries, although many jurisdictions have now legalized gambling. As it is available online, it is accessible almost anywhere, at any time, even in places where gambling is prohibited.>

Gambling can lead to serious harms to health. These include financial stress, relationship breakdown, family violence, mental illness and suicide. The legacy of gambling harm can endure throughout one’s life and transmit intergenerationally. Population-wide interventions can help prevent and reduce harm. These include ending advertising and promotions, providing centralized account registration to require those who gamble to set binding loss limits, and restrictions relating to access and availability (opening hours, density). Strict regulation and enforcement are also required to ensure compliance with existing laws.

sections.heading: Scope of the problem
sections.text:
Gambling is now legally available in many countries. It has been normalized through new commercial associations with sport and cultural activities that are now heavily promoted. Around 5.5% of women and 11.9% of men globally experience some level of harm from gambling (3) . A Swedish study estimated that those with a gambling disorder were 15 times more likely to die by suicide than the general population (4) . In Victoria Australia, at least 4.2% of suicides were found to be gambling-related (5) .

For every person who gambles at high-risk levels, an average of six others (usually non-gamblers) are affected (6) . This number is likely much higher in kinship cultures, including among Indigenous peoples. Gambling may also divert normal consumption expenditure from other businesses.

Industry self-regulation is a common feature of gambling regulation. However, there are many examples of the failure of this approach. There is often little transparency about the way many gambling products function. EGMs can mislead users with design features that encourage extended use. Existing health promotion messages are often inadequate and can use so-called dark nudges, which encourage the consumption of harmful products (for example, by exploiting gamblers' cognitive biases) and may enhance normalization. Alongside strong regulation of gambling products and their availability, clear warning messages about harms associated with use are likely to be more effective than messages suggestions to simply stop when gambling is no longer fun, for instance.

There is no global agreement on the regulation of online gambling. Unlicensed providers regularly offer unregulated gambling products, and there is an urgent need for the regulation of online gambling.

sections.heading: Who is at risk?
sections.text: People experiencing significant life events including separation, retirement, injury or the death of a loved one may be at increased risk. Social stressors such as poverty, discrimination or other disadvantage also increase risks. Heavy promotion of gambling online and through sport also poses risks of normalizing gambling for children and young people.

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text:
Gambling disorder is described alongside substance use disorders in both the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition (DSM 5), and the International Classification of Diseases, eleventh revision (ICD 11). The ICD-11 describes three diagnostic requirements:

1) impaired control over gambling;

2) increasing priority given to gambling, taking precedence over other life interests and daily activities; and

3) continuation of gambling despite negative consequences.

Gambling harm also occurs well below clinical thresholds. Signs of harm include the diversion of money from essential household spending. This can lead to food insecurity, housing problems and difficulties accessing healthcare and education.

sections.heading: Transmission
sections.text:
Easy accessibility of gambling products increases the risk of uptake. Opportunities to gamble are often disproportionately located in areas of higher disadvantage. High-intensity products including EGMs, high-speed wagering platforms, and casino games, including online versions, are readily accessible almost anywhere.

The commercialization of gambling in many countries – which also drives normalization – is increasing the incidence of gambling harm. Sponsorship or other association with popular sporting leagues, and the colocation of gambling products in social settings, are key mechanisms. Aggressive promotion of gambling in popular and social media also increases gambling activity.

sections.heading: Prevention and control
Treatment
sections.text:
A range of therapies exist for those with gambling disorder. Currently, the most effective are long-term cognitive behavioural therapy or motivational interviewing. Self-help, pharmacological interventions and mutual support have less evidence of efficacy, although the latter are among the most used interventions. Some evidence supports internet-based therapies, although attrition is a significant issue.

Treatment for gambling disorder has a low rate of uptake, with an estimated 0.14% of the population seeking formal and informal help for current problems. Stigma and shame often prevent people from seeking help. The preferred regulatory approach of the gambling industry – so-called responsible gambling – adds to this burden by effectively blaming those who experience harm. Responsible gambling interventions are typically ineffective, particularly where the uptake of measures is optional.

Those seeking to better control or cease gambling should be provided with tools to support them. These include universal pre-commitment (requiring people to set binding limits of time and money spent gambling) and self-exclusion (allowing people to ban themselves from gambling providers). Universal (also known as mandatory) systems are most effective. Voluntary systems have poor uptake and are non-enforceable. Prevention is the most cost-effective strategy for minimizing gambling-related harm.

sections.heading: Challenges
sections.text:
In countries where gambling has been legalized, governments typically receive substantial taxation revenues. This can create some dependence, creating disincentives to reduce harm. Perceived economic benefits of gambling markets may have precedence over poorly understood effects on health and well-being.

Gambling industry groups typically strongly oppose high-impact regulations and other measures that affect their commercial interests. Corporate political activity is widespread and effective in protecting the interests of these businesses. The research sector has also been influenced by industry using funding and other support. Limiting the capacity of vested interests to influence the research agenda and public policies are among the key public health objectives.

sections.heading: Global impact
sections.text: Gambling harm increases as gambling markets expand, challenging the health and well-being of populations. Unlicensed, illegal or offshore gambling poses significant regulatory challenges for all governments. Responding effectively requires intergovernmental cooperation to share data, protect consumers from unregulated practices and allow governments to capture lawful taxation revenue. Without effective protections, gambling may undermine progress toward the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly 3, 10 and 16.

sections.heading: WHO response
sections.text:
WHO recognizes negative effects of gambling on health. Multisectoral action to reduce gambling harm is required to reduce the potential for gambling to impede progress on SDGs. WHO acknowledges the need for Member States to closely monitor and effectively regulate gambling operations, products and activities. This should include reducing stigma and shame related to gambling, ending advertising and promotion, and a focus on other upstream efforts to prevent and reduce gambling harm.

WHO is coordinating a group of global experts to build capacity to address public health implications of gambling. Initial efforts include leading the development of new diagnostic instruments for gambling disorder to better reflect populations outside North America and facilitating an expert consensus on diagnostic boundaries. WHO recognizes that some jurisdictions have developed effective gambling regulatory systems. Efforts to document and distribute these lessons are underway, particularly to support low- and middle-income countries where commercial gambling activity is rapidly increasing.

sections.heading: 重要事实
sections.text:
• 对全球赌博危害的标准化研究工作还很有限，但据估计全世界1.2%成年人口面临赌博障碍。赌博对其他人造成危害的现象也很普遍。

• 行业分析师估计，到2028年，全球赌博收入将达到7000亿美元 (1) 。低收入和中等收入国家智能手机的普及将推动这一增长。

• 达到有害程度的赌博占总损失(赌博收入)约60% (2) 。

• 赌博会威胁健康，导致精神疾病和自杀的发生率增加。它会导致消耗家庭用于基本商品和服务的支出，从而加剧贫困。

• 赌博的危害还包括关系破裂、家庭暴力、财务困境、耻辱、取得型财产犯罪(盗窃、欺诈)、忽视儿童以及通过腐败和企业政治活动侵蚀民事机构。赌博也是一种常见的清洗非法活动所得资金的洗钱方式。

• 通过商业化和数字化，赌博正在迅速正常化。赞助和营销也是赌博活动全球快速增长的关键因素。

sections.heading: 概述
sections.text:
赌博是对结果不确定事件下注金钱或具物质价值的其它东西以赢取更多金钱和/或物质价值。投注、老虎机、各种赌场游戏、彩票和宾果游戏都是赌博的形式。电子赌博机和赌场游戏通常伤害风险最大。赌博活动可以发生在物理场所，也可以在线进行。尽管许多司法管辖区现在已经将赌博合法化，赌博的法律地位在国家内部和国家之间各不相同。赌博可以线上进行，因此几乎可以在任何地点、任何时间访问赌博网站，甚至在禁止赌博的地方。

赌博会对健康造成严重危害。这些包括经济压力、关系破裂、家庭暴力、精神疾病和自杀。赌博伤害的后果会贯穿一个人的一生，并代代相传。针对全民的干预措施有助于预防和减少伤害。这些措施包括消除赌博广告和促销，实施集中帐户注册，要求赌博者设置具有约束力的止损限额，并对网站访问和可用性（开放时间、密度）进行限制。还需要严格的监管和执法，以确保遵守现行法律。

sections.heading: 问题的范围
sections.text:
现在，赌博在许多国家都是合法的。赌博正常化进程是现在得到大力推广的体育和文化活动相关新商业协会推动的。全球约有5.5%女性和11.9%男性经历过赌博带来的某种程度的伤害 (3) 。瑞典一项研究估计，赌博成瘾者自杀的可能性是普通人群的15倍 (4) 。在澳大利亚维多利亚州，至少有4.2%的自杀事件与赌博有关 (5) 。

每个参与高风险赌博的人平均影响六个人（通常是不赌博的人） (6) 。这一数字在亲属文化（包括土著人民）中可能要高得多。赌博也会转移原本可用于其他领域的正常消费支出。

赌博监管的共同特征是靠行业自律。然而，这种方法失败的例子很多。许多赌博产品的运作方式往往缺乏透明度。电子赌博机被设计得鼓励长时间使用，可能会误导用户。现有的健康促进信息往往不足，可能使用所谓的暗推手段鼓励消费有害产品（例如，利用赌徒的认知偏见），并可能促进正常化。除严格监管赌博产品及其提供外，关于相关危害的明确警告信息可能比建议在赌博不再有趣时停下来的信息更有效。

没有关于在线赌博监管的全球协议。未经许可的提供商经常提供不受监管的赌博产品。迫切需要对在线赌博进行监管。

sections.heading: 谁面临风险？
sections.text: 经历重大生活事件（包括分居、退休、受伤或亲人死亡）的人可能面临更大风险。贫穷、歧视或其他不利条件等社会压力因素也会增加风险。大力推广在线赌博和通过体育运动进行赌博也会带来儿童和年轻人赌博行为正常化的风险。

sections.heading: 体征和症状
sections.text:
《精神障碍诊断和统计手册》第五版和《国际疾病分类》第十一次修订本有关赌博障碍的内容与物质使用障碍并列。《国际疾病分类》第十一次修订本描述了三条诊断标准：

1) 对赌博的控制能力减弱；

2) 越来越重视赌博，超过其他生活兴趣和日常活动；以及

3) 尽管有不良后果，但仍继续赌博。

也存在远低于临床阈值的赌博危害。危害的迹象包括从基本家庭支出中挪用资金。这可能导致粮食不安全、住房问题以及难以享受到医疗保健和教育服务。

sections.heading: 传播
sections.text:
赌博产品的容易获得增加赌博活动上升的风险。赌博机会往往不成比例地集中在面临更多不利因素的地区。高强度的产品，包括电子赌博机、高速投注平台和赌场游戏（包括在线版本），几乎可以从任何地方轻易访问。

在许多国家，赌博的商业化——这也推动了赌博的正常化——正在增加赌博危害的发生率。赞助或与流行体育联盟建立其他联系，以及在社交环境中托管赌博产品，是造成危害的主要机制。在大众和社交媒体上积极推销赌博也会增加赌博活动。

sections.heading: 预防与控制
sections.text:
需要普遍的、针对全人口的公共卫生方法来防止发生赌博危害。这其中包括：

• 消除赌博广告、促销及赞助体育和其他文化活动；

• 减少因赌博而受到伤害的人所经历的污名和羞辱；

• 实施普遍账户登记，包括有约束力的预先承诺和有效的自我排除工具；

• 产品安全措施，包括通用损失限额、最大投注额和赌博时段中的强制休息时间；

• 有效监管赌博活动提供者，包括资源充足的执法活动；

• 处理赌博企业的政治活动和对研究的影响；以及

• 发布对抗赌博的信息，对赌博产品相关危害发出警告。

sections.heading: 治疗
sections.text:
对于赌博障碍，存在一系列治疗方法。目前，最有效的是长期认知行为疗法或动机访谈。自助、药物干预和相互支持等疗法的有效性证据较少，不过后者是最常用的干预措施。一些证据支持基于互联网的治疗，不过自然减员是个重要问题。

赌博障碍的治疗率很低，估计只有0.14%正在受影响者寻求正式和非正式的帮助。污名和羞耻往往会阻止人们寻求帮助。赌博业的首选监管方法，即所谓负责任赌博，也就是指责那些遭受伤害的人，反过来加重了这种负担。负责任赌博相关干预通常无效，特别是在不强制实行的情况下。

那些寻求更好地控制或停止赌博的人应该获得支持他们的工具。这些措施包括普遍适用的预先承诺(要求人们设定有约束力的时间限制和赌博支出上限)和自我排除措施(允许人们禁止自己与赌博提供商接触)。普遍性(也称为强制性)制度最为有效。自愿制度的采用率很低，而且无法执行。预防是最具成本效益的减少赌博相关危害的策略。

sections.heading: 挑战
sections.text:
在赌博合法化的国家，政府通常会获得大量税收收入。这可能会产生某种依赖性，因而不愿减少危害。政府认为可以从赌博市场中获得经济效益，但对赌博对健康和福祉的影响知之甚少。

赌博业团体通常强烈反对影响其商业利益的影响很大的法规和其他措施。这些企业广泛开展政治活动，有效地保护了自己的利益。研究人员也受到企业利用资金和其他支持而产生的影响。公共卫生工作的主要目标之一就是限制既得利益集团影响研究议程和公共政策的能力。

sections.heading: 全球影响
sections.text: 赌博的危害随赌博市场扩大而增加，对人们的健康和福祉构成挑战。无牌、非法或离岸赌博对所有政府都构成重大监管挑战。有效应对需要政府间合作，以共享数据，保护消费者免受未监管做法的影响，并允许政府获得合法的税收。如果没有有效保护措施，赌博可能会破坏实现可持续发展目标的进展，特别是可持续发展目标3、10和16。

sections.heading: 世卫组织的应对
sections.text:
世卫组织认识到赌博对健康的负面影响。需要采取多部门行动减少赌博的危害，以减少赌博阻碍可持续发展目标取得进展。世卫组织承认会员国需要密切监测和有效监管赌博业务、产品和活动。这应该包括减少与赌博有关的污名和耻辱，停止广告和促销，并专注于其他预防和减少赌博危害的上游努力。

世卫组织正在协调一个全球专家小组，以建设应对赌博对公共卫生影响的能力。最初的努力包括领导开发新的赌博障碍诊断工具，以更好地反映北美以外人群的情况，并促进专家对诊断界限的共识。世卫组织认识到，一些管辖区已制定了有效的赌博监管制度。正在努力记录和传播这些经验教训，特别是支持商业赌博活动迅速增加的低收入和中等收入国家。

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a condition that happens when the immune system attacks the brain and spinal cord.

Symptoms of MS vary from person to person and depend on the location and severity of nerve fibre damage. These often include vision problems, tiredness, trouble walking and keeping balance, and numbness or weakness in the arms and legs. Symptoms can come and go or last for a long time.

The causes of MS are not known but a family history of the disease may increase the risk.

While there is no cure for MS, treatment can reduce symptoms, prevent further relapses and improve quality of life.

MS can present in a variety of ways including:

• clinically isolated syndrome (CIS): describes an episode of neurologic symptoms that are the first clinical sign of possible MS;

• relapsing remitting (RRMS): the most common form of MS characterized by intermittent attacks of symptoms (relapses), followed by a short or long period of no clinical attacks (remissions);

• secondary progressive (SPMS): after living with RRMS for a long period of time, relapses decrease and symptoms continue progressively without relapses or remissions; and

• primary progressive (PPMS): starting from the initial symptoms, the disease gradually progresses and gets worse without any clear relapses or remissions.

MS is not always easy to diagnose in its early stages. Typically, people who have been diagnosed with MS will have been through several diagnostic stages, which can be an unsettling and frightening experience.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text:
Symptoms of multiple sclerosis can be different from person to person. They can come and go or get worse over time. MS can affect any part of the central nervous system.

MS symptoms can worsen with heat or during other infections such as urinary tract or respiratory infections.

Symptoms can include:

• vision problems

• difficulty walking or keeping balance

• difficulty thinking clearly

• numbness or weakness especially in the arms and legs

• muscle stiffness

• depression

• problems with sexual function or urination

• feeling very tired.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.text:
MS is an inflammatory demyelinating condition that results from an autoimmune attack on myelin, the fatty insulation that surrounds the nerves in the brain and spinal cord. This disrupts the electrical impulses that are sent through the nerves to the rest of the body and results in scars (plaques or sclerosis).

It is not known what triggers the immune system to attack myelin, but genetic and environmental factors are thought to play a role. MS happens most commonly in young to middle-aged adults, more in females than males, and is more common in higher latitudes, possibly due to sun exposure and vitamin D.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.text: MS is a diagnosis of exclusion and there are no definitive diagnostic tests. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can help with diagnosis by showing plaques or sclerosis on the brain and spinal cord. Other tests such as lumbar puncture, optical coherence tomography (OCT) and visual evoked potentials can also help support the diagnosis.

sections.heading: Treatment and care
sections.text:
Treatments for MS will be different for each person. They depend on the stage of the disease and symptoms.

The goals of MS treatment are to reduce the frequency and severity of relapses, slow disease progression, manage symptoms, and improve quality of life.

Specific MS disease modifying therapies (DMTs) are started as early as possible to slow disease progression and prevent relapses.

Steroids are sometimes used in the short term to treat relapses. Other medicines can be used to reduce the symptoms of MS such as fatigue, muscle tightening, depression and urinary or sexual problems. These medicines do not change the course of the disease but help manage the symptoms.

Rehabilitation specialists can help improve functioning, quality of life and reduce muscle stiffness and spasms.

Many people feel fatigue with multiple sclerosis. Ways to manage fatigue include:

• regular exercise

• healthy sleep patterns

• avoiding medicines that make fatigue worse.

In the past twenty years treatment options for MS have improved dramatically. In high income countries many oral, intravenous and injectable options exist to treat MS. However, most of these medications are not available in low- and middle-income countries and there is still a lack of treatment options for progressive types of MS.

People with MS and their families should be encouraged to seek services and guidance from local and national Organizations of Disabled People (ODPs) and other disability focused organizations, which can provide vital advice about legal rights, economic opportunities and social engagement to ensure that people disabled by MS or other neurological disorders are able to live full and rewarding lives.

sections.heading: WHO Response
重要事实
sections.text:
• 多发性硬化症（MS）影响人的认知、情感、运动、感觉或视觉功能，是人体免疫系统攻击大脑和脊髓的结果。

• 据估计，全世界有180多万人患有多发性硬化症。

• 各个年龄段的人都可能罹患此病，但其在年轻人和女性中更为常见。

• 在多发性硬化症发病初期，可通过药物治疗改善或稳定病情。根据疾病的严重程度和症状不同，治疗方法因人而异。

sections.heading: 概述
sections.text:
多发性硬化症是免疫系统攻击大脑和脊髓时会出现的一种疾病。

多发性硬化症的症状因人而异，取决于神经纤维损伤的部位和严重程度。这些症状通常包括视力问题、疲倦、难以行走和保持平衡以及四肢麻痹或无力。症状可能时好时坏，也可能会持续很长时间。

多发性硬化症的病因尚不得而知，但家族病史会增加患病风险。

多发性硬化症虽无法治愈，却可通过治疗减轻症状、防止复发并提高生活质量。

多发性硬化症有多种表现形式，其中包括：

• 临床孤立综合征（CIS）：指神经系统症状的单次发作，这些症状则属于疑似罹患多发性硬化症的首个临床体征；

• 复发缓解型（RRMS）：是最常见的多发性硬化症类型，特征是症状间歇性发作（复发），并在随后的一段时间（可长可短）内，无临床发作（缓解）；

• 继发进展型（SPMS）：罹患复发缓解型多发性硬化症较长一段时间后，复发次数减少，但症状持续进展，而不再是复发或缓解；

• 原发进展型（PPMS）：从初期症状开始，病情逐渐进展、恶化，没有明显的复发或缓解。

多发性硬化症在早期阶段并非总能轻易确诊。通常情况下，被确诊为多发性硬化症的患者都会经历几个诊断阶段，这可能会是一次令人感到不安和恐惧的经历。

sections.heading: 症状
sections.text:
多发性硬化症的症状因人而异，可能时好时坏，或是随着时间的推移而加重。多发性硬化症可累及中枢神经系统的任何部位。

在高温或有其他感染（如尿路感染或呼吸道感染）的情况下，症状会有所加重。

这些症状包括：

• 视力问题

• 难以行走或保持平衡

• 难以清晰地思考

• 感觉麻痹或无力，尤其是四肢

• 肌肉僵硬

• 抑郁

• 性功能障碍或排尿困难

• 感到非常疲倦。

sections.heading: 病因
sections.text:
多发性硬化症是一种炎性脱髓鞘疾病，由自身免疫攻击髓鞘（即包裹在大脑和脊髓神经周围的脂肪绝缘体）所致。这会破坏通过神经发送至身体其他部位的电脉冲并留下疤痕（斑块或硬化）。

目前尚不清楚是什么触发了免疫系统对髓鞘的攻击，但遗传和环境因素被认为在其中发挥了一定作用。多发性硬化症最常见于中青年，女性多于男性，在高纬度地区更为常见，这可能与阳光照射和维生素D有关。

sections.heading: 诊断
sections.text: 多发性硬化症属排除性诊断，尚无明确的诊断性检查。磁性共振成像可显示大脑和脊髓中的斑块或硬化，有助诊断。其他一些检查，如腰椎穿刺、光学相干断层扫描和视觉诱发电位，也有助于为诊断提供支持。

sections.heading: 治疗和护理
sections.text:
多发性硬化症的治疗方法因人而异，取决于疾病所处阶段和症状。

多发性硬化症的治疗目标是降低复发的频率和严重程度，减缓疾病进展，控制症状，提高生活质量。

应尽早针对多发性硬化症，开始采用特定的疾病修饰疗法，以减缓疾病进展并防止复发。

有时，会在短期内使用类固醇来治疗复发。可使用其他药物来减轻多发性硬化症的症状，如疲劳、肌肉紧缩、抑郁、泌尿系统问题或性功能障碍。这些药物不会改变病程，但有助控制症状。

康复专家可帮助患者改善功能，提高生活质量，缓解肌肉僵硬和痉挛。

许多多发性硬化症患者都会感到疲劳。缓解疲劳的方法包括：

• 定期锻炼

• 健康的睡眠模式

• 避免服用会加重疲劳的药物。

过去二十年间，多发性硬化症的治疗方案得到了显著改善。在高收入国家，治疗多发性硬化症有多种选择，如口服方案、静脉注射方案和注射方案。然而，在低收入和中等收入国家，大多数此类药物都无法获得，对于进展型多发性硬化症，仍缺乏治疗方案。

应鼓励多发性硬化症患者及其家属寻求地方和国家残疾人组织以及其他关注残疾问题组织的服务和指导，这些组织可以提供关于法律权利、经济机会和社会参与的重要建议，以确保多发性硬化症或其他神经系统疾病致残者能够过上充实而有意义的生活。

sections.heading: 世卫组织的应对
sections.text:
2022年5月，世界卫生大会批准了《2022-2031年癫痫和其他神经系统疾病跨部门全球行动计划》。该行动计划将解决在为全世界癫痫和其他神经系统疾病（如多发性硬化症）患者提供护理和服务方面存在的许多挑战和不足，并确保采取跨部门的全面协调应对措施。这包括进一步重视政策和加强治理，提供有效、及时和反应灵敏的诊断、治疗和护理，实施促进和预防策略，推动研究与创新以及加强信息系统。

世卫组织还通过以下方式，支持各国管理多发性硬化症：

• 努力将多发性硬化症药物纳入世卫组织基本药物清单；

• 就广泛问题与多发性硬化症国际联合会等民间团体开展合作，并通过世界多发性硬化症日（5月30日）开展宣传工作；

• 制作《多发性硬化症地图集》，供多发性硬化症患者、卫生专业人员以及多发性硬化症团体和组织使用，以促进开展各种运动并为其提供信息，改善向多发性硬化症患者以及关心其福祉和生活质量的人提供的各种服务和支持；

• 支持各国实施指南和加强卫生系统，以改善为神经系统疾病患者提供的康复服务。

sections.heading: Key facts
sections.text:
• Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal disorder in which higher than normal androgen levels lead to irregular menstrual periods, abnormal ovulation, infertility, excess facial or body hair and/or acne in women (1).

• PCOS affects an estimated 10–13% of reproductive-aged women. It is estimated that up 70% of women with PCOS worldwide do not know they have this condition.

• PCOS is the most common cause of anovulation among women globally and a leading cause of infertility.

• PCOS runs in families but can cause a range of different symptoms and affect women in different ways. PCOS is a chronic metabolic condition that persists beyond the reproductive years.

• Women with PCOS are at higher risk for a variety of longer-term health problems that affect physical and emotional well-being compared to women without PCOS, including insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal disorder that affects women during their reproductive years and beyond, into later stages of life.

PCOS occurs when inappropriate hormonal signaling leads to higher than normal androgen levels and other hormonal imbalances. As a result, women with PCOS may experience irregular or infrequent menstrual periods, pain – including pain with heavy menstrual bleeding, abnormal ovulation, changes in hair (either excessive facial or body hair or female-pattern baldness), oilier skin, acne and/or cysts in the ovaries.

PCOS is a leading cause of irregular menstrual periods and one of the most common causes of infertility. Irregular or infrequent menstrual periods among women with PCOS may also raise their risk for endometrial hyperplasia and/or endometrial cancer. PCOS can start as early as during adolescence but is most commonly detected or diagnosed when women struggle to become pregnant.

Further, PCOS is a chronic metabolic condition associated with heightened long-term risk for insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity. There is currently no cure for PCOS, but lifestyle changes, medications and fertility treatments can reduce symptoms, increase fertility rates and protect longer-term health.

The cause of PCOS is unknown, but women with a family history of PCOS or type 2 diabetes are at higher risk.

sections.heading: Scope of the problem
sections.text:
PCOS a significant global public health problem and is one of the most common hormonal disorders affecting women, often becoming apparent during the reproductive years. An estimated 10–13% of women globally are thought to have PCOS, but up to 70% of affected women are undiagnosed.

The prevalence of PCOS may be higher among women in some racial or ethnic groups than others, and some women have higher genetic propensity for metabolic complications. However, structural racism and other social determinants of health shape the extent to which different groups of women with PCOS seek and receive quality health services.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.text:
Symptoms of PCOS can differ from person to person, and an individual’s symptoms may change over time.

Possible symptoms include:

• intermittent, unpredictable or absent periods; or, for some women, heavy or long and/or painful periods

• difficulty conceiving or infertility

• excessive hair on the face or body

• female-pattern baldness or hair thinning

• acne or oily skin.

Women with PCOS have an increased risk of developing other health conditions including:

• gestational diabetes or high blood pressure in pregnancy

• weight gain, especially around the belly

• type 2 diabetes

• hypertension (high blood pressure)

• high cholesterol

• cardiovascular disease

• obesity

• sleep apnea

• metabolic steatohepatitis

• endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial cancer (abnormal growth or cancer, respectively, of the inner lining of the uterus).

PCOS can adversely impact quality of life in substantial ways, and women with PCOS may experience anxiety, depression, eating disorders and/or a negative body image. Symptoms such as infertility, obesity and unwanted hair growth are subject to social stigma in many settings. This can affect social and family relationships, work, a sense of belonging in one’s community, mental health and other aspects of well-being.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.text:
PCOS is diagnosed by the presence of at least two of the following, once other causes for these symptoms have been excluded:

• signs or symptoms of high androgens (excess facial or bodily hair, loss of hair from the head, acne or oily skin) or an elevated blood level of testosterone;

• irregular or absent menstrual periods; and

• polycystic ovaries on an ultrasound in women.

This means that some women with PCOS do not have polycystic ovaries, and ovarian cysts are not required for PCOS diagnosis. Blood tests can be used to identify higher than normal levels of androgen steroids in women who do not have visible excess hair or acne or to check whether ovulation is occurring normally in women who might have PCOS but who have regular menstrual cycles. When making a PCOS diagnosis, health workers consider genetic risk factors since women with a family history of PCOS or type 2 diabetes are at higher risk of PCOS. Health workers also take life stage into account because irregular periods can be normal at either the beginning (menarche) or end (perimenopause) of the reproductive years.

Women who are newly diagnosed with PCOS are recommended to have additional blood testing to evaluate for underlying insulin resistance and to assess their overall cardiovascular risk.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text:
There is no cure for PCOS, but treatments can improve quality of life, assist with fertility, reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and/or endometrial cancer and help prevent long-term cardiovascular events. Seeking health care early to manage symptoms of PCOS can help women protect their health and well-being during and beyond their reproductive years.

Healthy lifestyle behaviors, including healthy eating and physical activity, are important for all women with PCOS, even if they do not lead to weight loss.

Combined oral contraceptive pills can help regulate the menstrual cycle and may reduce acne or excess facial and body hair. Androgen receptor blockers may also be used to treat excess hair or acne. Treatment choices should be based on shared decision-making, taking every individual’s unique values and preferences into account.

Treatments for infertility due to PCOS include lifestyle changes, medicines or surgery to stimulate ovulation. In-vitro fertilization (IVF) and other assistive reproductive technologies may also be used. Women with PCOS can be supported to become pregnant but generally have higher risk of pregnancy complications that warrants additional monitoring.

sections.heading: WHO response
sections.text:
WHO promotes research regarding prevention, diagnosis and treatment of infertility for women with PCOS as well as broader menstrual health, seeking to identify and elevate the most important unanswered related questions. WHO works with Member States and partners to address PCOS as part of its broad efforts to improve women’s health and well-being globally. WHO works with governmental and nongovernmental partners to enhance public awareness related to PCOS, and to generate guidance for health-care providers on how it can be recognized and treated.

WHO supports the generation of statistics on how common infertility and its causes (such as PCOS) are. WHO also helps Member States to pay more attention to infertility and its causes within national health policies, services and financing to ensure that everyone who needs health care related to infertility is able to obtain it without financial hardship.

1) In this fact sheet, the term “women” is used inclusively to refer to all women, girls and gender-diverse individuals who menstruate and who may therefore be at risk of developing PCOS at some point in their life.

sections.heading: 重要事实
sections.text:
• 多囊卵巢综合征（PCOS）是一种常见的激素失调症，雄激素水平高于正常水平会导致女性月经不规律、排卵异常、不孕、面部或身体毛发过多和/或痤疮(1)。

• 估计有10-13%的育龄女性患有多囊卵巢综合症。据估计，全球高达70%患多囊卵巢综合症的女性不知道自己患有这种疾病。

• 多囊卵巢综合征是全球女性不排卵的最常见原因，也是不孕的主要原因。

• 多囊卵巢综合症具有家族遗传性，但会引起一系列不同的症状，并以不同的方式影响女性。多囊卵巢综合症是一种慢性代谢疾病，持续到生殖年龄之后。

• 与未患多囊卵巢综合症的女性相比，患有多囊卵巢综合症的女性出现各种影响身心健康的长期健康问题的风险更高，包括胰岛素抵抗、2型糖尿病和肥胖。

sections.heading: 概述
sections.text:
多囊卵巢综合征（PCOS）是一种常见的激素失调症，影响育龄期及以后的女性，直至生命的晚期。

当不适当的激素信号导致高于正常的雄激素水平和其他激素失衡时，就会发生多囊卵巢综合症。因此，患有多囊卵巢综合症的女性可能会出现月经不规律或稀发、疼痛——包括疼痛伴月经大量出血、排卵异常、头发变化（面部或身体毛发过多或女性秃头）、皮肤油性、痤疮和/或卵巢中的囊肿。

多囊卵巢综合征是月经不调的主要原因，也是不孕的最常见原因之一。患有多囊卵巢综合症的女性月经不规律或稀发也可能增加她们患子宫内膜增生和/或子宫内膜癌的风险。多囊卵巢综合症最早可以在青春期开始，但最常见的是在女性难以怀孕时被发现或诊断出来。

此外，多囊卵巢综合征是一种慢性代谢疾病，与胰岛素抵抗、2型糖尿病和肥胖的长期风险升高相关。目前还没有治愈多囊卵巢综合症的方法，但生活方式的改变、药物和生育治疗可以减轻症状、提高生育率并保护长期健康。

多囊卵巢综合征的病因尚不清楚，但有多囊卵巢综合征或2型糖尿病家族史的女性风险较高。

sections.heading: 问题的范围
sections.text:
多囊卵巢综合症是一个重大的全球公共卫生问题，也是影响女性最常见的激素失调症之一，通常在生育期变得明显。据估计，全球有10-13%的女性被认为患有多囊卵巢综合症，但高达70%的受影响女性未得到诊断。

多囊卵巢综合症的患病率在某些种族或民族的女性中可能高于其他人，并且一些女性具有更高的代谢并发症遗传倾向。然而，结构性种族主义和其他健康问题的社会决定因素决定了患有多囊卵巢综合症的不同妇女群体寻求和获得优质卫生服务的程度。

sections.heading: 症状
sections.text:
多囊卵巢综合症的症状因人而异，并且一个人的症状可能会随着时间的推移而变化。

可能的症状包括：

• 月经断断续续、无规律或停经；或者对一些女性来说，月经量大、经期长和/或经期疼痛

• 怀孕困难或不孕

• 面部或身体毛发过多

• 女性型秃顶或头发稀疏

• 痤疮或油性皮肤。

患有多囊卵巢综合症的女性出现其他健康问题的风险增加，包括：

• 妊娠期糖尿病或妊娠期高血压

• 体重增加，尤其是腹围

• 2型糖尿病

• 高血压

• 高胆固醇

• 心血管疾病

• 肥胖症

• 睡眠呼吸暂停

• 代谢性脂肪性肝炎

• 子宫内膜增生或子宫内膜癌（分别是子宫内膜的异常生长或癌症）。

多囊卵巢综合症会对生活质量产生重大不利影响，患有多囊卵巢综合症的女性可能会出现焦虑、抑郁、饮食失调和/或负面的身体形象。在许多情况下，不孕、肥胖和毛发过度生长等一些症状会导致社会污名。这会影响社会和家庭关系、工作、对社区的归属感、心理健康和福祉的其他方面。

sections.heading: 诊断
sections.text:
多囊卵巢综合症通过存在以下至少两种情况来诊断，但需排除导致这些症状的其他原因：

• 高雄激素的体征或症状（面部或身体毛发过多，脱发，痤疮或油性皮肤）或血液中睾酮水平升高；

• 月经不规律或闭经；以及

• 超声扫描显示多囊卵巢。

这意味着一些患有多囊卵巢综合症的女性不存在多囊卵巢的情况，多囊并非诊断多囊卵巢综合征所必需的条件。血检可用于确定没有明显毛发过多情况或痤疮的女性体内的雄激素类固醇水平是否高于正常水平，或用于检查可能患有多囊卵巢综合征但月经周期正常的女性是否正常排卵。在进行多囊卵巢综合症的诊断时，卫生工作者会考虑遗传风险因素，因为有多囊卵巢综合症或2型糖尿病家族史的女性患多囊卵巢综合症的风险更高。卫生工作者还会考虑到人生阶段，因为在生育期的初期（初潮）或末期（围绝经期）月经周期不规律是正常现象。

建议新诊断出患有多囊卵巢综合症的女性进行额外的血液检测，以评估潜在的胰岛素抵抗和整体的心血管风险。

sections.heading: 治疗
sections.text:
多囊卵巢综合症无法治愈，但治疗可以改善生活质量，帮助生育，降低子宫内膜增生和/或子宫内膜癌的风险，并有助于预防长期心血管事件。尽早就医以控制多囊卵巢综合症的症状可以帮助女性在生育期及以后保护自己的健康和福祉。

健康的生活方式，包括健康饮食和身体活动，对于所有患多囊卵巢综合症的女性来说都很重要，即使这些习惯不会导致体重减轻。

复合口服避孕药可以帮助调节月经周期，并可能减少痤疮或过多的面部和身体毛发。雄激素受体阻滞剂也可用于治疗毛发过多或痤疮。治疗选择应该基于共同决策，考虑每个人的独特价值观和偏好。

对多囊卵巢综合征所致不孕症的治疗包括改变生活方式、药物或手术以刺激排卵。还可以使用体外受精（IVF）和其他辅助生殖技术。可以支持患多囊卵巢综合症的女性怀孕，但通常出现妊娠并发症的风险较高，需要进行额外的监测。

sections.heading: 世卫组织的应对
sections.text:
世卫组织促进关于患多囊卵巢综合征妇女不孕症的预防、诊断和治疗以及更广泛的月经健康的研究，寻求确定并突出那些尚未得到解答的、重要的相关问题。世卫组织与会员国和伙伴合作应对多囊卵巢综合征问题，作为其改善全球妇女健康和福祉的广泛努力的一部分。世卫组织与政府和非政府伙伴合作，提高公众对多囊卵巢综合征的认识，并就如何识别和治疗多囊卵巢综合征向卫生保健服务提供者提供指导。

世卫组织支持生成关于不孕症的普遍程度及其原因（如多囊卵巢综合征）的统计数据。世卫组织还帮助会员国在国家卫生政策、服务和筹资中更加关注不孕症及其原因，以确保每个需要不孕症相关卫生保健服务的人都能获得这种服务而不会遭遇经济困难。

(1) 在本实况报道中，“女性”一词泛指所有来月经并因此在人生的某个阶段可能面临患多囊卵巢综合症风险的女性、女童和性别多样化的人。

sections.heading: Key facts
sections.text:
• El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is one of the most important sources of annual global climate variability, second only to the earth–sun relationship that drives the seasons. El Niño and its counterpart La Niña are associated with characteristic patterns of rainfall and temperature, which can include extreme events such as flooding and drought.

• ENSO affects many parts of the globe, but most intensely impacts the tropics, including countries and areas in Africa, Latin America and South and South-East Asia that are particularly vulnerable to natural hazards.

• By altering climate conditions, ENSO can have severe effects on key health determinants through, among other factors, impacts on food security, air and water quality, ecosystems and health infrastructure safety. ENSO is also associated with altered transmission patterns of vector-borne, rodent-borne and waterborne diseases, as well as fish and shellfish poisoning.

• Early warning systems and anticipatory action can help reduce the impacts of extreme weather conditions exacerbated by ENSO.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a naturally occurring large-scale climatic phenomenon involving fluctuating ocean temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, coupled with changes in the overlying atmosphere. El Niño and La Niña are the oceanic components, while the Southern Oscillation is the atmospheric counterpart, thus giving rise to the term El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). ENSO occurs in irregular cycles of 2–7 years and presents 3 phases: El Niño, La Niña and a neutral phase. An El Niño event is characterized by a period of sea-surface warming and consequent suppression of the nutrient-rich cold water up-welling off the coast of Peru and Ecuador, typically lasting between 12 and 18 months. In contrast, a La Niña event is characterized by a period of colder than average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean and an intensification of the prevailing east to west surface winds.

sections.heading: ENSO and climate
sections.text:
The effects of each El Niño/La Niña event vary depending on the intensity, duration, time of year when it develops, and the interaction with other modes of climate variability. Not all regions of the world are affected, and even within a region, impacts can be different. Along with increased global temperatures, common regional influences of El Niño include:

• Africa : drier conditions in southern Africa and some areas in the Sahel; wetter conditions in equatorial east Africa during the short rainy season (October–December);

• Asia Pacific, central Asia : lower rainfall in South and South-East Asia; wetter conditions in the eastern-central Pacific islands and across the Hindu Kush mountain range in central Asia; and

• Latin America : drier conditions in northern Brazil; heavy rainfall in Central America, northern Peru, Ecuador, and the northern and southeastern parts of South America.

El Niño and rainfall – map

La Niña impacts tend to be opposite those of El Niño, with cooler global temperatures and:

• Africa : wetter than normal conditions in southern Africa; drier than normal conditions over equatorial east Africa (December to February);

• Asia Pacific, central Asia : higher than normal rainfall in countries including Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines; reduced rainfall in central Asia (January to May); and

• Latin America : wetter than normal conditions over northern Brazil; drier than normal conditions along the central and eastern Pacific coasts; a more active hurricane season in the Caribbean.

La Niña and rainfall - map

sections.heading: Health impacts
sections.text:
Local incidence of vector-borne diseases, wildfire smoke exposure, heat stress, drought-related health and nutritional impacts have all been observed to be influenced by ENSO events.

Observed associations between ENSO and health impacts are not linear or unequivocal but depend on the ENSO intensity, time of the year and other factors. Impacts tend to be more intense in less developed countries where populations have limited coping capacity and are often more vulnerable to the impacts of extreme weather and climate. Their livelihoods are often highly dependent on natural resources and rain-fed agricultural practices; housing typically lacks protection against extreme weather events; access to health care and safe drinking-water and adequate sanitation facilities may be limited; and infectious diseases determined by environmental conditions are often pre-existing.

sections.heading: Vector-borne diseases
sections.text: Vectors, such as mosquitoes, that are responsible for the transmission of malaria, dengue and Rift Valley fever are sensitive to changes in temperature, rainfall and humidity, which determine the suitability of ecosystems for vector reproduction, development and activity.

sections.heading: Malaria
sections.text: The effects of ENSO on malaria are most pronounced in epidemic-prone areas where climate conditions are generally not suitable for year-round vector reproduction. Small changes in climate conditions in these areas have the potential to change normally unsuitable habitats into viable habitats for mosquitoes that transmit malaria, or to temporarily extend the period of malaria susceptibility. The effect of ENSO on malaria is mediated by its impact on rainfall and temperature patterns. In dry areas, intense rainfall can create water puddles; in wet areas, drought can result in reservoirs of stagnant water, both of which are conducive to generation of new mosquito breeding sites. Decreased immunity acquired over time by inhabitants of these new malaria-prone areas can further increase the risk of outbreaks. Evidence of the association between ENSO and malaria has been found in southern Africa, South Asia and South America.

sections.heading: Air pollution
sections.text:
ENSO-related drought conditions can increase the risk of wildfires resulting in local and trans-boundary smoke pollution. The inhalation of fire smoke is a major public health problem, causing respiratory diseases and other harmful effects.

The El Niño-related drought of 1997 contributed to the exacerbation of forest fires in Brazil, Indonesia and Malaysia. In 2015, air quality in 6 South-East Asian countries was impacted by wildfires exacerbated by El Niño-related drought, including Indonesia where a state of emergency was declared due to hazardous air quality.

sections.heading: Extreme heat
sections.text:
Any transition from a La Niña to an El Niño phase will likely produce a rise in global average surface temperature, with warming tendencies affecting the development of extreme heat in the Southern Hemisphere. The joint influence of both El Niño warming and rising global temperatures caused by climate change amplifies the potential for extreme heat in many regions, creating deadly conditions for millions of people.

Learn more about heat and climate change

sections.heading: Drought and food insecurity
sections.text:
Food production is extremely sensitive to climate conditions. ENSO-related droughts and heavy rainfalls can therefore jeopardize food security. Some of the worst food crisis events have been associated with ENSO.

• The world food crisis of 1982–84, the most severe recorded, was also linked to El Niño, including famines that struck populations in the Horn of Africa and the Sahel.

• El Niño triggered the 1991–1992 drought in southern Africa, affecting nearly 100 million people.

• In Peru, a study found that children born during and after 1997–1998 El Niño, while controlling for other factors, were on average shorter and had less lean mass for their age and sex than expected had El Niño not occurred.

• A so-called triple dip La Niña event in 2020–23 resulted in 3 consecutive years of drought in Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia, leaving millions of people facing severe hunger.

• Droughts in Brazil, north-east China, Indonesia, Marshall Islands, Papua New Guinea, and the Philippines have also been associated with ENSO.

sections.heading: Health preparedness
sections.text:
ENSO events can be predicted with some reliability several months in advance, allowing the climate community to prepare seasonal forecasts with enhanced precision. The increased predictability of climate events on seasonal to inter-annual timescales can help planners and health professionals anticipate, prepare for and respond to ENSO-related health risks. For example:

• In 2014, ENSO-related information produced by the International Research Institute for Climate and Society (IRI) for the malaria community in east Africa, provided time-sensitive information for interventions to reduce malaria transmission in high-risk areas.

• Countries where Enhanced National Climate Services (ENACTS) are being developed can share information on the past impacts of ENSO events, particularly related to the spatial and temporal distribution of rainfall and temperature changes at the district level.

sections.heading: WHO response
sections.text:
WHO protects human health from risks related to climate variability through its programmes on environmental and social determinants of health, emergency preparedness and response, infectious disease prevention and control, improving health research and evidence, and health system strengthening.

In accordance with mandates from the World Health Assembly, WHO supports countries to develop national strategies and plans of action to build health system resilience to climate change, to improve awareness and evidence of local climate impacts on health, as well as strengthening health system capacity to manage consequent health risks of extreme weather and climate change.

A joint WHO/World Meteorological Office (WMO) office for climate and health was established in 2014. This office supports WHO to improve health preparedness and decision making through enhanced use of weather and climate information, including in relation to ENSO.

sections.heading: 重要事实
sections.text:
• 厄尔尼诺/南方涛动（ENSO）是全球年度气候变化的最重要原因之一，仅次于驱动季节的地球/太阳关系。厄尔尼诺及其对应的拉尼娜涉及有特征的降雨和温度模式，其中可包括洪水和干旱等极端事件。

• 厄尔尼诺/南方涛动影响全球许多地区，但对热带地区的影响最为强烈，包括非洲、拉丁美洲、南亚和东南亚特别容易受到自然灾害影响的国家和地区。

• 通过改变气候条件，厄尔尼诺/南方涛动会因为对粮食安全、空气和水质、生态系统和卫生基础设施安全性等因素的影响，对关键的健康决定因素产生严重影响。厄尔尼诺/南方涛动还与病媒传播疾病、啮齿动物传播疾病和水源性疾病以及鱼类和贝类中毒的传播模式改变有关。

• 早期预警系统和预防行动有助于减少由厄尔尼诺/南方涛动加剧的极端天气情况的影响。

sections.heading: 概述
sections.text: 厄尔尼诺/南方涛动（ENSO）是一种自然发生的大规模气候现象，涉及赤道太平洋中部和东部的海洋温度波动，以及上空的大气层的变化。厄尔尼诺和拉尼娜涉及海洋，而南方涛动是大气的对应现象，因此产生了厄尔尼诺/南方涛动（ENSO）一词。厄尔尼诺/南方涛动以2-7年的不规则周期发生，呈现3个阶段：厄尔尼诺、拉尼娜和中性阶段。厄尔尼诺事件的特征是一段时间内的海面变暖，随之而来的是秘鲁和厄瓜多尔海岸营养丰富的冷水上升流受到抑制，通常持续12至18个月。相比之下，拉尼娜事件的特征是太平洋中部和东部一段时间内的海面温度低于平均温度，并且盛行的东向西海面风力增强。

sections.heading: 厄尔尼诺/南方涛动与气候
sections.text:
每次厄尔尼诺/拉尼娜事件的影响取决于其强度、持续时间、一年中出现的时间以及与其他气候变化模式的相互作用。并非世界上所有地区都受到影响，即使在一个地区内，影响也可能不同。随着全球气温升高，厄尔尼诺的常见区域影响包括：

• 非洲： 南部非洲和萨赫勒部分地区天气较干燥；东非赤道地区在短暂的雨季（10月至12月）雨量增多；

• 亚太、中亚： 南亚和东南亚的降雨量减少；太平洋中东部岛屿和中亚兴都库什山脉的雨量增多；

• 拉丁美洲： 巴西北部天气较干燥；中美洲、秘鲁北部、厄瓜多尔以及南美洲北部和东南部地区有强降雨。

厄尔尼诺和降雨 – 地图 （英文）

拉尼娜 的影响往往与厄尔尼诺相反，全球气温较低，并且：

• 非洲： 南部非洲的降雨量比正常情况更多；东非赤道地区比正常情况更干燥（12月至2月）；

• 亚太、中亚： 印度尼西亚、马来西亚和菲律宾等国的降雨量多于正常水平；中亚降雨量减少（1月至5月）；

• 拉丁美洲： 巴西北部的降雨量比正常情况更多；太平洋中部和东部沿岸比正常情况更干燥；加勒比地区有更活跃的飓风季节。

拉尼娜和降雨 – 地图 （英文）

sections.heading: 对健康的影响
sections.text:
据观察，当地病媒传播疾病的发病率、野火烟雾暴露、热应激、与干旱有关的健康和营养影响都受到厄尔尼诺/南方涛动事件的影响。

厄尔尼诺/南方涛动与健康影响之间观察到的关联不是线性的或明确的，而是取决于厄尔尼诺/南方涛动的强度、一年中出现的时间和其他因素。在较不发达国家，人口的应对能力有限，常常更容易受到极端天气和气候的影响，因此影响往往更为严重。在那里，人们的生计常常高度依赖自然资源和靠雨水灌溉的耕作方法；住房通常不能应对极端天气事件；获得卫生保健、安全饮用水和适当环境卫生设施的机会可能有限；而且常常原本就存在由环境条件决定的传染病。

sections.heading: 病媒传播疾病
sections.text: 导致疟疾、登革热和裂谷热传播的蚊虫等病媒对温度、降雨量和湿度的变化很敏感，这些变化决定了生态系统是否适合病媒繁殖、发育和活动。

sections.heading: 疟疾
sections.text: 厄尔尼诺/南方涛动对疟疾的影响在流行易发地区最为明显，因为那里的气候条件通常不适合病媒全年繁殖。这些地区气候条件的微小变化有可能将通常不适宜的生活环境转变为对传播疟疾的蚊子有利的生活环境，或者会暂时延长疟疾易感期。厄尔尼诺/南方涛动对疟疾的影响取决于其对降雨和温度模式的影响。在干旱地区，强降雨会形成水坑；在潮湿地区，干旱会导致不流动的积水，这两者都有利于产生新的蚊虫滋生地。免疫力随着时间的推移会有所下降，所以这些新的疟疾易发地区的居民会面临进一步加大的疫情暴发风险。在南部非洲、南亚和南美洲发现了厄尔尼诺/南方涛动与疟疾之间关联的证据。

sections.heading: 空气污染
sections.text:
与厄尔尼诺/南方涛动相关的干旱情况会加大野火的风险，可导致当地和跨境烟雾污染。吸入火灾烟雾是一个重大的公共卫生问题，会导致呼吸系统疾病和其他有害影响。

1997年与厄尔尼诺有关的干旱加剧了巴西、印度尼西亚和马来西亚的森林火灾。2015年，6个东南亚国家的空气质量受到因厄尔尼诺相关干旱加剧的野火的影响，其中包括印度尼西亚，该国因有害的空气质量而宣布进入紧急状态。

sections.heading: 酷热
sections.text:
从拉尼娜到厄尔尼诺阶段的任何转变都可能导致全球平均地表温度上升，变暖趋势会影响南半球极端高温的形成。厄尔尼诺变暖和气候变化导致的全球气温上升的共同影响加大了许多地区极端高温的可能性，对数百万人形成了可危及生命的恶劣环境。

了解关于高温和气候变化的更多信息（英文）

sections.heading: 干旱和粮食不安全
sections.text:
粮食生产对气候条件极为敏感。因此，与厄尔尼诺/南方涛动相关的干旱和强降雨会危及粮食安全。一些最严重的粮食危机事件与厄尔尼诺/南方涛动有关。

• 1982-84年的世界粮食危机是有记录以来最严重的一次，也与厄尔尼诺有关，包括影响非洲之角和萨赫勒地区人口的饥荒。

• 厄尔尼诺引发了1991-1992年南部非洲的干旱，影响了近1亿人。

• 在秘鲁，一项研究发现，在控制其他因素的情况下，与没有厄尔尼诺发生情况下预计的年龄和性别身高体重相比，1997-1998年厄尔尼诺期间和之后出生的儿童平均身高较矮，肌肉量也较少。

• 2020-23年所谓的三重拉尼娜事件导致埃塞俄比亚、肯尼亚和索马里连续3年干旱，使数百万人面临严重饥饿。

• 巴西、中国东北部、印度尼西亚、马绍尔群岛、巴布亚新几内亚和菲律宾的干旱也与厄尔尼诺/南方涛动有关。

sections.heading: 卫生防范
sections.text:
厄尔尼诺/南方涛动事件可以提前几个月进行一定程度的可靠预测，使气候界能够更精确地制定季节性预报。在季节性到年际时间尺度上提高气候事件的可预测性，可以帮助规划者和卫生专业人员预测、防范和应对与厄尔尼诺/南方涛动相关的健康风险。例如：

• 2014年，国际气候与社会研究所（IRI）为东非疟疾社区提供的厄尔尼诺/南方涛动相关信息为减少高风险地区疟疾传播的干预措施提供了及时信息。

• 正在创建加强型国家气候服务部门（ENACTS）的国家可以分享有关厄尔尼诺/南方涛动事件以往影响的信息，特别是与区县级降雨和温度变化的空间和时间分布情况有关的信息。

sections.heading: 世卫组织的应对
sections.text:
世卫组织通过其关于健康问题环境和社会决定因素、突发事件防范和应对、传染病预防和控制、改进卫生研究和证据以及加强卫生系统等方面的规划，保护人类健康免受与气候变化有关的风险。

根据世界卫生大会的授权，世卫组织支持各国制定国家战略和行动计划，以建立对气候变化有抵御能力的卫生系统，巩固关于当地气候对健康影响的认识和证据，并加强卫生系统管理极端天气和气候变化带来的健康风险的能力。

2014年成立了世卫组织/世界气象组织（WMO）气候与健康联合办公室。该办公室支持世卫组织通过加强利用天气和气候信息，包括与厄尔尼诺/南方涛动相关的信息，改进卫生防范和决策。

sections.heading: Key facts
sections.text:
• Each year, an estimated 400 000 children and adolescents of 0–19 years old develop cancer (1) .

• The most common types of cancer affecting children include leukemias, brain tumours and solid tumours such as neuroblastoma and Wilms tumour; lymphomas, bone cancer and thyroid cancer are more common during adolescence.

• In high-income countries, where comprehensive services are generally accessible, more than 80% of children with cancer are cured. In most low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), less than 30% are cured (2) .

• Avoidable deaths from childhood cancers in LMICs result from lack of diagnosis, misdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis, obstacles to accessing care, abandonment of treatment, death from toxicity and relapse (2) .

• Only 29% of low-income countries report that cancer medicines are generally available to their populations compared to 96% of high-income countries.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
Cancer is a leading cause of death for children and adolescents. The likelihood of surviving a diagnosis of childhood cancer depends on the country in which the child lives; in high-income countries, more than 80% of children with cancer are cured, but in many LMICs less than 30% are cured (2) .

Although childhood cancer cannot generally be prevented or identified through screening, most types of childhood cancer can be cured with generic medicines and other forms of treatment, including surgery and radiotherapy.

The reasons for lower survival rates in LMICs include delay in diagnosis, an inability to obtain an accurate diagnosis, inaccessible therapy, abandonment of treatment, death from toxicity (side effects) and avoidable relapse. Improving access to childhood cancer care, including to essential medicines and technologies, is highly cost-effective, feasible and can improve survival in all income settings .

Childhood cancer data systems are needed to drive continuous improvements in the quality of care, and to inform policy decisions.

sections.heading: Causes
sections.text:
Cancer occurs in people of all ages and can affect any part of the body. It begins with genetic change in single cells, that can then grow into a mass (or tumour), invade other parts of the body and cause harm and death if left untreated. Unlike cancer in adults, most childhood cancers do not have a known cause. Many studies have sought to identify the causes of childhood cancer, but very few cancers in children are caused by environmental or lifestyle factors. Cancer prevention efforts in children should focus on behaviours that will prevent the child from developing preventable cancer as an adult.

Some chronic infections, such as HIV, Epstein-Barr virus and malaria, are risk factors for childhood cancer. They are particularly relevant in LMICs. Other infections can increase a child’s risk of developing cancer as an adult, so it is important to be vaccinated (against hepatitis B to help prevent liver cancer and against human papillomavirus to help prevent cervical cancer) and to other pursue other methods such as early detection and treatment of chronic infections that can lead to cancer.

Current data suggest that approximately 10% of all children with cancer have a predisposition because of genetic factors (3) . Further research is needed to identify factors impacting cancer development in children.

sections.heading: Improving outcomes of childhood cancer
sections.text: Because it is generally not possible to prevent cancer in children, the most effective strategy to reduce the burden of cancer in children and improve outcomes is to focus on a prompt, correct diagnosis followed by effective, evidence-based therapy with tailored supportive care.

sections.heading: Early diagnosis
sections.text:
When identified early, cancer is more likely to respond to effective treatment and result in a greater probability of survival, less suffering, and often less expensive and less intensive treatment. Significant improvements can be made in the lives of children with cancer by detecting cancer early and avoiding delays in care. A correct diagnosis is essential to treat children with cancer because each cancer requires a specific treatment regimen that may include surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy.

Early diagnosis consists of 3 components:

• awareness of symptoms by families and primary care providers;

• accurate and timely clinical evaluation, diagnosis, and staging (determining the extent to which a cancer has spread); and

• access to prompt treatment.

Early diagnosis is relevant in all settings and improves survival for many cancers. Programmes to promote early and correct diagnosis have been successfully implemented in countries of all income levels, often through the collaborative efforts of governments, civil society and nongovernmental organizations, with vital roles played by parent groups. Childhood cancer is associated with a range of warning symptoms, such as fever, severe and persistent headaches, bone pain and weight loss, that can be detected by families and by trained primary health-care providers.

Screening is generally not helpful for childhood cancers. In some select cases, it can be considered in high-risk populations. For example, some eye cancers in children can be caused by a mutation that is inherited, so if that mutation or disease is identified in the family of a child with retinoblastoma, genetic counselling can be offered and siblings monitored with regular eye examinations early in life. Genetic causes of childhood cancers are relevant in only a small proportion children with cancer. There is no high-quality evidence to support population-based screening programmes in children.

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text:
A correct diagnosis is essential to prescribe appropriate therapy for the type and extent of the disease. Standard therapies include chemotherapy, surgery and/or radiotherapy. Children also need special attention to their continued physical and cognitive growth and nutritional status, which requires a dedicated, multi-disciplinary team. Access to effective diagnosis, essential medicines, pathology, blood products, radiation therapy, technology and psychosocial and supportive care are variable and inequitable around the world.

However, cure is possible for more than 80% of children with cancer when childhood cancer services are accessible. Pharmacological treatment, for example, includes inexpensive generic medications included on the WHO List of essential medicines for children . Children who complete treatment require ongoing care to monitor for cancer recurrence and to manage any possible long-term impact of treatment.

sections.heading: Palliative care
sections.text:
Palliative care relieves symptoms caused by cancer and improves the quality of life of patients and their families. Not all children with cancer can be cured, but relief of suffering is possible for everyone. Paediatric palliative care is considered a core component of comprehensive care, starting when the disease is diagnosed and continuing throughout treatment and care, regardless of whether a child receives treatment with curative intent.

Palliative care programmes can be delivered through community and home-based care, providing pain relief and psychosocial support to patients and their families. Adequate access to oral morphine and other pain medicines should be provided for the treatment of moderate to severe cancer pain, which affects more than 80% of cancer patients in the terminal phase.

sections.heading: WHO response
sections.text:
In 2018, WHO launched, with the support of St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, the Global Initiative for Childhood Cancer (Global Initiative), to provide leadership and technical assistance to governments to support them in building and sustaining high-quality childhood cancer programmes. The goal is to achieve at least 60% survival for all children with cancer by 2030. This represents an approximate doubling of the current cure rate and will save an additional 1 million lives over the next decade.

The CureAll framework and its accompanying technical package have been developed to support implementation of the Initiative. The package helps governments and other stakeholders assess current capacity, set priorities, generate investment cases, develop evidence-based standards of care and monitor progress. An information-sharing portal has been created to facilitate sharing of expertise between countries and partners.

The Global Initiative is part of the response to the World Health Assembly resolution Cancer Prevention and Control through an Integrated Approach (WHA70.12), focused on the reduction of premature mortality from NCDs and the achievement of universal health coverage.

In December 2021, WHO and St Jude Children’s Research Hospital launched the Global Platform for Access to Childhood Cancer Medicines (Global Platform), the first of its kind, to provide an uninterrupted supply of quality-assured childhood cancer medicines with end-to-end support from selecting to dispensing medicines according to best possible care standards. The Global Platform synergizes with the Global Initiative, with activities implemented through this new effort expected to contribute substantially to the achievement of the initiative’s goals.

WHO and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) collaborate with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and other UN organizations and partners, to:

• increase political commitment for childhood cancer control;

• support governments to develop high-quality cancer centres and regional satellites to ensure early and accurate diagnosis and effective treatment;

• develop standards and tools to guide the planning and implementation of interventions for early diagnosis, treatment and palliative and survivorship care,

• improve access to essential medicines and technologies; and

• support governments to safeguard families of children with cancer from financial harm and social isolation as a result of cancer care.

References

• Steliarova-Foucher E, Colombet M, Ries LAG, et al. International incidence of childhood cancer, 2001-10: a population-based registry study. Lancet Oncol. 2017;18(6):719-731.

• Lam CG, Howard SC, Bouffet E, Pritchard-Jones K. Science and health for all children with cancer. Science. 2019 Mar 15;363(6432):1182-1186. doi: 10.1126/science.aaw4892. PMID: 30872518.

• Zhang J, Walsh MF, Wu G, Edmonson MN, Gruber TA, et al. Germline Mutations in Predisposition Genes in Pediatric Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2015 Dec 10;373(24):2336-2346.

sections.heading: 重要事实
sections.text:
• 每年 估计 有40万名0-19岁儿童和青少年罹患癌症 (1) 。

• 影响儿童的最常见癌症类型包括白血病、脑癌和实体瘤，如神经母细胞瘤和肾母细胞瘤；淋巴瘤、骨癌和甲状腺癌在青少年时期更为常见。

• 在可以普遍获得全面服务的高收入国家，80%以上的癌症患儿能得到治愈。在大多数低收入和中等收入国家，不到30%的患儿得到治愈 (2) 。

• 在低收入和中等收入国家，可避免的儿童癌症导致的死亡主要源自缺乏诊断，误诊或延迟诊断，难以获得治疗，放弃治疗，死于毒性作用以及疾病复发 (2) 。

• 仅有29%的低收入国家 报告 称，其人口通常可以获得癌症药物，而在高收入国家这一比例为96%。

sections.heading: 问题
sections.text:
癌症是儿童和青少年死亡的一个主要原因。儿童癌症确诊后存活的可能性取决于儿童生活的国家；在高收入国家，80%以上的癌症患儿能得到治愈，但在许多低收入和中等收入国家，只有不到30%得到治愈 (2) 。

虽然通常不能通过筛查来预防或识别儿童癌症，但大多数类型的儿童癌症可以通过仿制药和其他形式的治疗，包括手术和放疗来治愈。

在低收入和中等收入国家存活率较低的原因包括：诊断延迟，无法获得准确的诊断，无法获得治疗，放弃治疗，死于毒性（副作用）以及可避免的复发。进一步普及儿童癌症护理，包括提供基本药物和技术，具有很高的成本效益和可行性，可以提高所有 收入环境 中的存活率。

需要建立儿童癌症数据系统来推动持续改善护理质量并为政策决定提供信息。

sections.heading: 原因
sections.text:
癌症发生在所有年龄段的人身上，可以影响身体的任何部位。癌症始于单个细胞的基因变异，随后这些变异细胞会逐渐形成肿块（或肿瘤），侵入身体的其他部位，如果不进行治疗，会造成伤害和死亡。与成人癌症不同，大多数儿童癌症的确切病因尚不明确。许多研究都试图查明儿童癌症的原因，但很少有儿童癌症是因环境或生活方式因素所引起。儿童中的癌症预防工作应侧重于行为，以防止儿童成年后罹患可预防的癌症。

一些慢性感染，如艾滋病毒、爱泼斯坦-巴尔病毒和疟疾，是儿童癌症的危险因素，尤其对低收入和中等收入国家具有重要影响。其他感染会增加儿童成年后罹患癌症的风险，因此重要的是接种疫苗（例如接种乙肝疫苗以帮助预防肝癌，接种人乳头状瘤病毒疫苗以帮助预防宫颈癌）和采取其他方法，如早期发现和治疗可能导致癌症的慢性感染。

目前的数据表明，近10%的癌症患儿由于遗传因素而具有易感性 (3) 。需要开展进一步研究以确定影响儿童癌症发展的因素。

sections.heading: 改善儿童癌症的结局
sections.text: 由于通常不可能预防儿童癌症，因此减轻儿童癌症负担和改善预后的最有效策略是注重迅速、正确地做出诊断，然后进行有效的循证治疗和量身定制的支持性护理。

sections.heading: 早期诊断
sections.text:
如果及早发现，癌症更有可能对有效治疗产生反应，从而提高存活概率，减少痛苦，通常治疗也更便宜，并可减少强化治疗。通过及早发现癌症和避免延误治疗，可以显著改善癌症患儿的生活。正确的诊断对于治疗癌症患儿至关重要，因为每种癌症都需要特定的治疗方案，包括手术，放疗和化疗。

早期诊断 包括3部分：

• 家人和初级保健提供者意识到症状；

• 准确和及时地进行临床评估、诊断和分期（即确定癌症扩散的程度）；以及

• 获得及时治疗。

早期诊断在所有环境中都很重要，能提高许多癌症的存活率。通过政府、民间社会和非政府组织的共同努力，在各种收入水平的国家都成功开展了促进早期和正确诊断的规划，其中父母发挥了至关重要的作用。家人和受过培训的初级卫生保健提供者可以发现一系列与儿童癌症相关的预兆性症状，如发热、持续的剧烈头痛、骨痛和体重减轻。

筛查通常对儿童癌症没有帮助。在某些特定情况下，可以考虑在高风险人群中进行筛查。例如，儿童的一些眼癌可能是由遗传的某种突变引起的，因此如果在视网膜母细胞瘤患儿的家庭中发现该突变或疾病，可以提供遗传问题咨询服务，并在生命早期阶段通过定期的眼科检查监测兄弟姐妹的情况。儿童癌症的遗传原因仅与少部分癌症患儿有关。目前没有高质量的证据支持在儿童中开展基于人口的筛查规划。

sections.heading: 治疗
sections.text:
正确的诊断对于根据疾病的类型和程度确定适当的疗法至关重要。标准疗法包括化疗、手术和/或放疗。此外，还需要特别关注儿童的持续身体和认知发育以及营养状况，这需要一个专门的多学科团队。世界各地在获得有效的诊断、基本药物、病理分析、血液制品、放疗、技术以及社会心理支持服务方面存在差异和不平等。

然而，如果能够获得儿童癌症服务，80%以上的癌症患儿都有可能痊愈。例如，药物治疗包括 《世卫组织儿童基本药物清单》 中所列的廉价仿制药。完成治疗的儿童需要持续护理以监测癌症复发情况并管理可能因治疗造成的任何长期影响。

sections.heading: 姑息治疗
sections.text:
姑息治疗能缓解癌症引起的症状，提高患者及其家人的生活质量。并非所有癌症患儿都可以治愈，但每个人都可以减轻痛苦。儿科姑息治疗被视为综合护理的一个核心组成部分，从疾病确诊时即开始，并且无论儿童是否接受以治愈为目的的治疗，都应贯穿整个治疗和护理过程。

姑息治疗规划可以通过社区和家庭护理来实施，为患者及其家人提供缓解疼痛的办法和社会心理支持。应该提供足够的口服吗啡和其它止痛药以治疗80%以上的癌症末期患者承受的中度至重度癌症疼痛。

sections.heading: 世卫组织的反应
sections.text:
2018年，世卫组织在圣裘德儿童研究医院的支持下发起了 《全球儿童癌症倡议》 ，目的是提供领导和技术援助，以支持各国政府建立和维持高质量的儿童癌症规划。目标是到2030年使所有癌症患儿的生存率至少达到60%。这相当于目前治愈率的近两倍，并将在未来十年内额外挽救100万人的生命。

CureAll框架 及其配套技术包是为支持实施全球倡议而开发的。该技术包帮助各国政府和其它利益攸关方评估当前能力、确定优先事项、提出投资理由、制定循证护理标准和监测进展。已经建立了一个信息共享门户，以促进国家和合作伙伴之间分享专门知识。

《全球儿童癌症倡议》是为响应世界卫生大会题为“结合综合性方法审视癌症预防和控制”的决议（WHA70.12）而采取的一项行动，该决议的重点是减少非传染性疾病导致的过早死亡以及实现全民健康覆盖。

2021年12月，世卫组织和圣裘德儿童研究医院推出了首个 全球儿童癌症药物获取平台 ，目的是不间断地提供有质量保证的儿童癌症药物，并根据最佳护理标准提供从药物选择到配药的端到端支持。全球平台与全球倡议协同增效，通过这一新的努力开展的活动预计将大大有助于实现该倡议的目标。

世卫组织和 国际癌症研究机构 与 国际原子能机构 以及其他联合国组织和伙伴合作：

• 强化对儿童癌症控制的政治承诺；

• 支持各国政府发展高质量的癌症中心和地区分支机构，以确保早期的准确诊断和有效治疗；

• 为指导规划和实施干预措施制定标准和开发工具，以促进早期诊断、治疗和姑息治疗以及生存关怀；

• 改善基本药物和技术的获取机会；以及

• 支持政府保护癌症患儿的家庭，防止其因癌症治疗而遭受经济损失和社会孤立。

参考文献

• Steliarova-Foucher E, Colombet M, Ries LAG, et al. International incidence of childhood cancer, 2001-10: a population-based registry study. Lancet Oncol. 2017;18(6):719-731.

• Lam CG, Howard SC, Bouffet E, Pritchard-Jones K. Science and health for all children with cancer. Science. 2019 Mar 15;363(6432):1182-1186. doi: 10.1126/science.aaw4892. PMID: 30872518.

• Zhang J, Walsh MF, Wu G, Edmonson MN, Gruber TA, et al. Germline Mutations in Predisposition Genes in Pediatric Cancer. N Engl J Med. 2015 Dec 10;373(24):2336-2346.

sections.heading: Fact sheet
sections.text: Key facts In 2024, an estimated 4.9 million children under the age of 5 years died worldwide, equivalent to one death every 6 seconds. Neonatal deaths (the first 28 days of life) accounted for 2.3 million deaths, representing 47% of all under‑five deaths. The global under‑five mortality rate (U5MR) declined to 37.4 deaths per 1000 live births in 2024, less than half its level in 2000. Progress in reducing under‑five mortality has slowed markedly since 2015, with stagnation in the total number of under‑five deaths between 2022 and 2024. Sub‑Saharan Africa and Southern Asia together accounted for more than 80% of all under‑five deaths in 2024, despite representing less than 60% of global live births. Children born in sub‑Saharan Africa remain at the highest risk, with a U5MR of 71.6 deaths per 1000 live births, nearly 14 times higher than in Europe and Northern America. The leading causes of under‑five death are preterm birth complications, intrapartum‑related events (birth asphyxia/trauma), pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria, all of which are largely preventable or treatable. Overview Substantial progress has been made in reducing child mortality over the past three decades. Since 1990, the global under‑five mortality rate has declined by approximately 60%, reflecting expanded access to immunization, improved nutrition, better management of childhood illnesses and wider availability of skilled health personnel at birth. However, most progress occurred prior to 2015. Between 2015 and 2024, the annual rate of reduction in under‑five mortality fell by more than half compared with 2000–2015. The total number of under‑five deaths has stagnated in recent years, remaining at roughly 4.8–4.9 million annually since 2022. This trend is particularly concerning given the large number of deaths due to preventable causes. Nearly half of all under‑five deaths now occur in the neonatal period, reflecting slower declines in neonatal mortality compared with mortality among children aged 1–59 months. Prematurity, intrapartum events (birth asphyxia/trauma), lower respiratory infections (pneumonia) and sepsis were the most common causes of mortality among neonates – accounting for almost 8 in 10 neonatal deaths. Preventing newborn deaths requires quality antenatal, intrapartum and postnatal care, including access to skilled health personnel at birth and essential newborn care. Child survival prospects remain deeply unequal. In 2024, more than four in five under-five deaths worldwide occurred in sub-Saharan Africa (2.8 million, 58 per cent of under-five deaths) and Southern Asia (1.2 million, 25 per cent of under-five deaths), underscoring the geographic concentration of the global child mortality burden. Fragile and conflict‑affected settings and low‑income countries face particularly high risks, driven by weak health systems, limited access to essential services, poverty and population growth. If current trends continue, more than 27 million children are projected to die before reaching their fifth birthday between 2025 and 2030, most from preventable causes. Who is most at risk? There are fewer countries with extremely high under-five mortality, but they are primarily located in sub-Saharan Africa. In 2024, only three countries – Niger, Nigeria and Somalia – had U5MRs above 100 deaths per 1000 live births, down from 41 countries in 2000. Newborns in settings without access to quality care at birth. The vast majority of newborn deaths take place in low and middle-income countries. Children living in fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCS) face substantially higher mortality rates. In 2024, children in FCS countries faced a U5MR nearly three times higher than children in non-FCS countries. Children from the poorest households, rural areas, and those born to mothers with limited education. Under-five mortality was approximately 1.5 times higher in rural than urban areas, and higher risks were associated with young maternal age, shorter birth intervals, and high birth order. What can be done? Ending preventable child deaths requires: strengthening health systems, particularly maternal, newborn and child health services; ensuring skilled health personnel at birth and quality newborn care; expanding prevention and treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria; improving nutrition, water and sanitation; and protecting child health investments, especially in high‑burden and fragile settings. Families should be advised to: seek prompt medical care if necessary (danger signs include feeding problems, or if a newborn or young child has reduced activity, difficulty breathing, a fever, fits or convulsions, or feels cold); register all births; and bring babies for timely vaccination according to national schedules.

documents.title: 儿童健康：面临新的威胁

sections.heading: 概述
sections.text:
近几十年来，尽管儿童的生存、营养和教育状况有了显著改善，但在所有可持续发展目标中，儿童健康和福祉指标的进展目前处于停滞不前的状态。在促进每个儿童的发展、确保他们有一个健康未来方面，目前没有一个国家提供了足够的条件。

今天，0至18岁儿童和青少年面临着一系列新的威胁。这些新的威胁涉及到气候变化、污染、有害商业营销、不健康生活方式和饮食、伤害和暴力、冲突、移徙和不平等，他们面临着不确定的未来，应对这些威胁急需采取紧急行动。

保护儿童和确保他们的未来需采取以下重要行动：

• 将儿童置于与可持续发展目标议程相关的每项政策的核心；

• 采取紧急行动减少温室气体排放，应对气候危机；

• 在政府最高层的协调下采取多部门行动；

• 在儿童问题上加大资助力度，从政治上优先考虑儿童问题；

• 让儿童和青年参与他们的未来设计；

• 颁布新的有关遏制有害商业营销的国家和国际条例，包括一份《联合国儿童权利公约》任择议定书；

• 改善关于儿童健康和福利数据的报告状况。

投资于儿童的健康、教育和福利为社会带来可观回报。在儿童问题上每投资一美元，许多干预措施的收益约为10美元，某些干预措施的收益可达20美元。在卫生领域每投资一美元，就会给中低收入国家带来20倍的收益，给低收入国家带来9倍的收益。改善儿童时期的健康和福祉，对儿童本人一生及其后代都大有益处。

sections.heading: 主要卫生风险 / 环境威胁
sections.text:
温室气体排放而导致的气候变化威胁着所有儿童的生命。海平面上升、极端天气事件、水和粮食无保障、高温、新出现的传染病和大规模人口迁移，都威胁着儿童当今的生活和未来的生存。今天，亿万儿童已受到这些问题的影响。

需采取紧急行动减少碳排放，以将全球气温上升幅度控制在1.5摄氏度以下，并执行2016年就气候变化签署的《巴黎协定》的规定。

室内和环境（室外）空气污染每年致700万人死亡（2016年）。空气污染与儿童呼吸道健康状况不佳有关，给儿童的肺部和大脑造成损害，增加儿童患心血管疾病、肥胖症、2型糖尿病和代谢综合征的风险。

全球约40%的儿童生活在非正规住区，他们所面临的与气候变化相关的卫生风险更为严重。在这些住区中，存在着住房不合标准、过度拥挤、地点危险、生活环境不健康、贫穷和难以获得基本服务等问题，给住区儿童的健康和福祉带来损害。

sections.heading: 肥胖症与非传染性疾病
sections.text:
儿童肥胖症的快速上升是21世纪最严重的公共卫生挑战之一，肥胖儿童和青少年的数量增加了10倍以上，从1975年的1100万增加到2016年的1.24亿。

儿童经常接触有害商业营销，他们每年可以看到数万条推销成瘾物质和不健康商品的广告，包括推销导致肥胖症和慢性病的快餐和含糖饮料广告。此外，在线赌博也会损害儿童的社交生活、学习成绩和心理健康。

母乳代用品（配方奶）产业年产值高达700亿美元。母乳代用品的不当使用与儿童智力低下、肥胖、糖尿病和其它非传染性疾病风险的增加有关，给社会造成3020亿美元的损失。

• 证据表明，某些国家的儿童一年仅在电视上看到的广告就多达3万条，其中许多是推销有害产品的广告。

• 一个对拉丁美洲23项研究的综述分析表明，超重和肥胖的家庭和儿童喜好和购买不健康食品与食品广告有关。

• 对巴西、中国、印度、尼日利亚和巴基斯坦的5岁和6岁儿童进行的抽样调查显示，68%的儿童能够识别至少一个香烟品牌标志，该比例在俄罗斯是50%，在中国是86%。

• 一项针对美国加利福尼亚州洛杉矶市11-14岁青少年的研究表明，非裔美国青年平均每天接触4.1个酒精广告。

• 伊朗儿童电视节目中，食品广告主要推销对口腔健康有潜在危害的食品，英国儿童电视节目中近三分之二的食品广告也是如此。

商业对儿童健康的威胁被危险地低估了。当企业出于商业目的把儿童作为目标买卖儿童个人资料时，儿童在网上的高曝光率也会对他们造成伤害。儿童还可能因暴露于网络欺凌和剥削，以及接触到网络犯罪分子和性侵犯者而受到伤害。

sections.heading: 伤害、暴力和冲突
sections.text:
道路伤害是导致5至29岁儿童和青少年死亡的主要原因。每年超过10亿儿童（占儿童总数的一半）遭受暴力侵害。

2018年，由于冲突、暴力、不平等和缺乏机会，国内流离失所人员、国际移民或难民已经迁移或正在迁移的人数达10亿之多，其中包括许多儿童。

sections.heading: 世卫组织的应对
sections.text:
2010年，世界卫生大会就向儿童推销食品和非酒精饮料问题通过了一系列建议（ WHA63.14号决议 ）。世界卫生大会批准了一套 12项建议 ，呼吁采取全球行动，禁止向儿童推销富含饱和脂肪、反式脂肪酸、游离糖或盐的食品和饮料。

2017年，世卫组织西太平洋地区通过了 WPR/RC68.R3号决议 ——《保护儿童免受食品营销的有害影响》。该决议呼吁加快采取多部门和多方利益攸关方行动，分享最佳做法，提供技术支持并开展宣传，加强各国在衡量和减轻食品营销有害影响方面的合作。

2020年，世卫组织-联合国儿童基金会-柳叶刀委员会根据全球40多名儿童卫生专家给出的专业意见，发表了题为《 世界儿童的未来？ 》的报告。报告阐述了儿童健康和福祉所面临的新威胁，并就确保儿童当今和未来健康提出建议。

世卫组织和联合国儿童基金会正在向各国提供技术支持，并在全球范围内就上述报告的结论和传达的信息进行交流和宣传。除其他外，世卫组织将：

• 与会员国合作，制定一份新的具有法律约束力并定期加以监督的《儿童权利公约》任择议定书，以遏制快餐、加糖饮料、母乳代用品不当使用、酒精和烟草等有害商业推销，并整理汇集最佳做法。

• 制定一套儿童卫生干预措施，必要时让其他部门共同参与；

• 采用系统化程序，为制定政策和规划生成和获取证据；

• 向各国儿童卫生规划提供综合技术支持；

• 与合作伙伴共同编制一个计分卡，用以监督报告中各项建议的执行情况。

sections.heading: Fact sheet
sections.text: Key facts In 2024, an estimated 4.9 million children under the age of 5 years died worldwide, equivalent to one death every 6 seconds. Neonatal deaths (the first 28 days of life) accounted for 2.3 million deaths, representing 47% of all under‑five deaths. The global under‑five mortality rate (U5MR) declined to 37.4 deaths per 1000 live births in 2024, less than half its level in 2000. Progress in reducing under‑five mortality has slowed markedly since 2015, with stagnation in the total number of under‑five deaths between 2022 and 2024. Sub‑Saharan Africa and Southern Asia together accounted for more than 80% of all under‑five deaths in 2024, despite representing less than 60% of global live births. Children born in sub‑Saharan Africa remain at the highest risk, with a U5MR of 71.6 deaths per 1000 live births, nearly 14 times higher than in Europe and Northern America. The leading causes of under‑five death are preterm birth complications, intrapartum‑related events (birth asphyxia/trauma), pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria, all of which are largely preventable or treatable. Overview Substantial progress has been made in reducing child mortality over the past three decades. Since 1990, the global under‑five mortality rate has declined by approximately 60%, reflecting expanded access to immunization, improved nutrition, better management of childhood illnesses and wider availability of skilled health personnel at birth. However, most progress occurred prior to 2015. Between 2015 and 2024, the annual rate of reduction in under‑five mortality fell by more than half compared with 2000–2015. The total number of under‑five deaths has stagnated in recent years, remaining at roughly 4.8–4.9 million annually since 2022. This trend is particularly concerning given the large number of deaths due to preventable causes. Nearly half of all under‑five deaths now occur in the neonatal period, reflecting slower declines in neonatal mortality compared with mortality among children aged 1–59 months. Prematurity, intrapartum events (birth asphyxia/trauma), lower respiratory infections (pneumonia) and sepsis were the most common causes of mortality among neonates – accounting for almost 8 in 10 neonatal deaths. Preventing newborn deaths requires quality antenatal, intrapartum and postnatal care, including access to skilled health personnel at birth and essential newborn care. Child survival prospects remain deeply unequal. In 2024, more than four in five under-five deaths worldwide occurred in sub-Saharan Africa (2.8 million, 58 per cent of under-five deaths) and Southern Asia (1.2 million, 25 per cent of under-five deaths), underscoring the geographic concentration of the global child mortality burden. Fragile and conflict‑affected settings and low‑income countries face particularly high risks, driven by weak health systems, limited access to essential services, poverty and population growth. If current trends continue, more than 27 million children are projected to die before reaching their fifth birthday between 2025 and 2030, most from preventable causes. Who is most at risk? There are fewer countries with extremely high under-five mortality, but they are primarily located in sub-Saharan Africa. In 2024, only three countries – Niger, Nigeria and Somalia – had U5MRs above 100 deaths per 1000 live births, down from 41 countries in 2000. Newborns in settings without access to quality care at birth. The vast majority of newborn deaths take place in low and middle-income countries. Children living in fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCS) face substantially higher mortality rates. In 2024, children in FCS countries faced a U5MR nearly three times higher than children in non-FCS countries. Children from the poorest households, rural areas, and those born to mothers with limited education. Under-five mortality was approximately 1.5 times higher in rural than urban areas, and higher risks were associated with young maternal age, shorter birth intervals, and high birth order. What can be done? Ending preventable child deaths requires: strengthening health systems, particularly maternal, newborn and child health services; ensuring skilled health personnel at birth and quality newborn care; expanding prevention and treatment of pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria; improving nutrition, water and sanitation; and protecting child health investments, especially in high‑burden and fragile settings. Families should be advised to: seek prompt medical care if necessary (danger signs include feeding problems, or if a newborn or young child has reduced activity, difficulty breathing, a fever, fits or convulsions, or feels cold); register all births; and bring babies for timely vaccination according to national schedules.

sections.heading: 重要事实
sections.text:
• 2024年，估计全球490万五岁以下儿童死亡，相当于每6秒就有1人死亡。

• 新生儿死亡（出生后28天内）为230万，占所有五岁以下死亡人数的47%。

• 2024年，全球五岁以下儿童死亡率下降至每千例活产37.4例死亡，不到2000年的一半。

• 自2015年以来，降低五岁以下儿童死亡率的进展明显放缓。2022年至2024年间，五岁以下儿童死亡总数大致持平。

• 2024年，撒哈拉以南非洲和南亚地区加起来占所有五岁以下死亡人数的80%以上，尽管这两个地区仅占全球活产婴儿的60%。

• 撒哈拉以南非洲出生的儿童仍然面临最高风险，每千例活产五岁以下儿童死亡71.6例，几乎是欧洲和北美的14倍。

• 五岁以下儿童死亡的主要原因是早产并发症、产时相关事件（出生时窒息/创伤）、肺炎、腹泻和疟疾，所有这些在很大程度上都可以预防或治疗。

sections.heading: 概述
sections.text:
过去三十年在降低儿童死亡率方面取得了重大进展。自1990年以来，全球五岁以下儿童死亡率下降约60%，原因是免疫接种机会扩大、营养改善、儿童疾病得到更好的管理以及出生时更广泛利用熟练卫生人员。

不过，大部分进展发生在2015年之前。2015年至2024年间，五岁以下儿童死亡率的年下降率与2000年至2015年相比减少一半以上。近年来，五岁以下儿童死亡总数大致持平，自2022年以来保持在每年480万至490万人左右。鉴于众多死亡由本可预防的原因造成，这一趋势尤其令人担忧。

目前，近一半五岁以下儿童死亡发生在新生儿期。也就是说，新生儿死亡率与1-59月龄儿童死亡率相比下降速度较慢。早产、产时事件（出生时窒息/创伤）、下呼吸道感染（肺炎）和败血症是最常见的新生儿死亡原因，几乎占新生儿死亡的十分之八。预防新生儿死亡需要优质的产前、产时和产后护理，包括在出生时获得熟练卫生人员帮助和基本新生儿护理。

儿童生存前景仍然严重不平等。2024年，全球五分之四以上五岁以下儿童死亡发生在撒哈拉以南非洲（280万，占58%）和南亚（120万，占25%），突出表明全球儿童死亡负担集中在特定地域。脆弱和受冲突影响环境和低收入国家面临的风险特别高，其原因是卫生系统薄弱、获得基本服务的机会有限、贫困和人口增长。

如果当前趋势继续下去，预计2025年至2030年间将有超过2700万儿童在五岁生日之前死亡，其中大多数死于可预防原因。

sections.heading: 谁面临最大风险？
sections.text:
五岁以下儿童死亡率极高的国家较少，主要位于撒哈拉以南非洲。2024年，只有尼日尔、尼日利亚和索马里这三个国家每千例活产儿童死亡人数超过100名，低于2000年时的41个国家。

出生时无法获得优质护理的新生儿。绝大多数新生儿死亡发生在低收入和中等收入国家。

生活在脆弱和受冲突影响环境的儿童面临高得多的死亡率。2024年，脆弱和受冲突影响国家的五岁以下儿童死亡率几乎是其它国家的三倍。

来自最贫困家庭、农村地区以及受教育程度有限的母亲所生的孩子。农村五岁以下儿童死亡率约为城市地区的1.5倍，而较高风险与产妇年龄较轻、出生间隔较短和胎次较高有关。

sections.heading: 可以做些什么？
sections.text:
结束可预防的儿童死亡需要：

• 加强卫生系统，特别是孕产妇、新生儿和儿童健康服务；

• 确保熟练卫生人员提供分娩时护理和优质新生儿护理；

• 扩大肺炎、腹泻和疟疾的预防和治疗；

• 改善营养、水和卫生设施；以及

• 保护儿童健康投资，特别是在高负担和脆弱环境中。

应建议家庭：

• 如有必要，立即就医（危险迹象包括喂养问题，或者新生儿或幼儿活动减少、呼吸困难、发烧、痉挛或抽搐或感觉寒冷）；

• 登记所有出生情况；以及

• 按照国家程序表及时带婴儿接种疫苗。

documents.title: Corporal punishment of children and health

sections.heading: Key facts
sections.text:
• Globally, an estimated 1.2 billion children aged 0–18 years are subjected to corporal punishment at home each year.

• In some countries, almost all students report being physically punished by school staff. The risk of being physically punished is similar for boys and girls, and for children from wealthy and poor households.

• Evidence shows corporal punishment harms children’s physical and mental health, increases behavioural problems over time, and has no positive outcomes.

• All corporal punishment, however mild or light, carries an inbuilt risk of escalation. Studies suggest that parents who used corporal punishment are at heightened risk of perpetrating severe maltreatment.

• Corporal punishment is linked to a range of negative outcomes for children across countries and cultures, including physical and mental ill-health, impaired cognitive and socio-emotional development, poor educational outcomes, increased aggression and perpetration of violence.

• Corporal punishment is a violation of children’s rights to respect for physical integrity and human dignity, health, development, education and freedom from torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

• The elimination of violence against children is called for in several targets of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development but most explicitly in Target 16.2: “end abuse, exploitation, trafficking and all forms of violence against and torture of children”.

• Corporal punishment and the associated harms are preventable through multisectoral and multifaceted approaches, including law reform, changing harmful norms around child rearing and punishment, parent and caregiver support, and school-based programming.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
Corporal or physical punishment is defined by the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, which oversees the Convention on the Rights of the Child , as “any punishment in which physical force is used and intended to cause some degree of pain or discomfort, however light.”

According to the Committee, this mostly involves hitting (smacking, slapping, spanking) children with a hand or implement (whip, stick, belt, shoe, wooden spoon or similar) but it can also involve, for example, kicking, shaking or throwing children, scratching, pinching, biting, pulling hair or boxing ears, forcing children to stay in uncomfortable positions, burning, scalding or forced ingestion.

Other non-physical forms of punishment can be cruel and degrading. They are also incompatible with the Convention. Punishments that belittle, humiliate, denigrate, scapegoat, threaten, scare or ridicule children often accompany and overlap with physical punishment.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text:
Globally 1.2 billion children aged 0–18 years are subjected to corporal punishment in the home each year. Some 17% of children have experienced severe physical punishment – such as being hit on the head, face or ears or hit hard and repeatedly – in the past month. The wide differences across countries, regions, and time periods indicate that much of this burden is preventable and that significant gains can be achieved through targeted action.

Apart from some countries where rates among boys are higher, results from comparable surveys show that the prevalence of corporal punishment is similar for girls and boys. Young children (aged 2–4 years) are as likely, and in some countries more likely, as older children (aged 5–14 years) to be exposed to physical punishment, including harsh forms.

Most children are exposed to both physical and psychological means of punishment. Many parents and caregivers report using non-violent disciplines measures (such as explaining why the child’s behaviour was wrong, taking away privileges) but these are usually used in combination with violent methods. Children who experience only non-violent forms of discipline are in the minority.

Studies have shown that lifetime prevalence of school corporal punishment was above 70% in Africa and Central America, past-year prevalence was above 60% in the WHO Regions of Eastern Mediterranean and South-East Asia ( 1 ). Lower rates were found in the WHO Western Pacific Region, with lifetime and past year prevalence around 25%. Physical punishment appeared to be highly prevalent at both primary and secondary school levels.

sections.heading: Consequences
Risk factors
WHO response
sections.text:
WHO addresses corporal punishment in multiple cross-cutting ways. In collaboration with partners, WHO provides guidance and technical support for evidence-based prevention and response. Work on several strategies from the INSPIRE technical package, including those on legislation, norms and values, parenting, and school-based violence prevention, contribute to preventing physical punishment. WHO also advocates for increased international support for and investment in these evidence-based prevention and response efforts.

References

(1) Heekes SL, Kruger CB, Lester SN, Ward CL. A systematic review of corporal punishment in schools: global prevalence and correlates. Trauma Violence Abuse . 2020;23(1): 1524838020925787. ( https://doi.org/10.1177/1524838020925787 ).

sections.heading: 重要事实
sections.text:
• 在全球范围内，每年约有12亿0至18岁儿童在家中遭受体罚。

• 在一些国家，几乎所有学生都报告受到学校工作人员的体罚。无论是男孩，还是女孩，也不论是来自富裕家庭，还是来自贫穷家庭，儿童受到体罚的风险都差不多。

• 有证据显示，随着时间的推移，体罚会损害儿童的身体和精神健康，增加行为问题，并且体罚行为不会产生积极的结果。

• 所有体罚，无论多么轻微，都有升级的内在风险。研究表明，使用体罚的父母遭受严重虐待的风险更高。

• 在不同国家和文化中，体罚与儿童的一系列负面结果相关，包括身心健康不佳、认知和社会情感发育受到影响、学习成绩差、攻击性增加和实施暴力。

• 体罚行为侵犯了儿童的身体完整和人的尊严、健康、发育、教育以及免受酷刑和其他残忍、不人道或有辱人格的待遇或处罚的权利。

• 《2030年可持续发展议程》的几项具体目标呼吁消除暴力侵害儿童行为，但最明确的是具体目标16.2：“制止对儿童进行虐待、剥削、贩卖以及一切形式的暴力和酷刑”。

• 通过采取多部门和多方面的方法，包括修订法律、改变与儿童抚养和惩罚有关的有害规范、为父母和看护者提供支持以及实施校内规划，体罚和相关伤害是可以预防的。

sections.heading: 概述
sections.text:
负责监督实施 《儿童权利公约》 的联合国儿童权利委员会将体罚定义为“任何使用身体暴力并旨在造成某种程度的疼痛或不适的惩罚，无论多么轻微”。

据委员会称，这主要涉及用手或工具（鞭子、棍子、皮带、鞋子、木勺或类似工具）殴打（掌掴、扇、拍打）儿童，但也可能涉及踢、摇晃或扔儿童、抓、捏、咬、揪头发或打耳光、强迫儿童保持不舒服的姿势、烧伤、烫伤或强迫进食。

其他非肉体形式的惩罚可能是残忍和有辱人格的，也与《公约》不符。与贬低、羞辱、诋毁、成为替罪羊、威胁、恐吓或嘲笑儿童相关的惩罚，经常伴随体罚或与之重叠。

sections.heading: 范围
sections.text:
